mcqs.question: The definition of O(g(n)) includes a constant n₀. What does that constant let you ignore?
options: The behavior of the function on all inputs smaller than n₀
The constant factor multiplying the growth term
Any operation that runs in constant time
The difference between worst case and average case
mcqs.explanation: n₀ is the threshold past which the bound must hold, so everything below it is excluded — a function can be arbitrarily badly behaved on small inputs and still satisfy the bound. Ignoring the constant factor is what the other constant, c, is for; the two are often confused.

mcqs.question: An algorithm's exact step count is 3n² + 200n + 5000. Why is its complexity written as O(n²) rather than keeping the other terms?
options: Because lower-order terms are always negligible on modern hardware
Because the notation only permits a single term by convention
Because as n grows the n² term eventually dominates the total, and the coefficients depend on the machine rather than the algorithm
Because 200n and 5000 are constant-time operations
mcqs.explanation: The n² term outgrows everything else, so past some input size the rest is rounding error — and coefficients like 3 or 200 shift with language and CPU while the growth class does not. It isn't a formatting convention, and 200n is emphatically not constant time.

mcqs.question: Is the statement "merge sort is O(n²)" true?
options: No — O gives a tight bound, so only O(n log n) is valid
Yes — O is an upper bound and n² is a valid, if uselessly loose, ceiling
No — merge sort's worst case is O(n log n), so a larger bound is false
Yes, but only when the input array is already sorted
mcqs.explanation: O asserts only "grows no faster than," so any function above the real growth is a technically true bound — n log n grows slower than n², so the claim holds. The tight bound Θ(n log n) is what an interviewer wants, which is why the true-but-loose answer still reads as a miss.

mcqs.question: Two functions are both O(1). What can you conclude about their running times?
options: They take the same amount of time on any given input
Both complete in a single machine instruction
Each is faster than any O(n) function on every input
Neither one's cost grows as the input grows, but one may be far slower than the other
mcqs.explanation: Constant time means independent of input size, not cheap or identical — a hash lookup and an array index are both O(1) while differing by dozens of instructions. And on small inputs an O(n) function can easily beat an O(1) one with a large constant.

mcqs.question: You need to sort batches of about 20 elements, millions of times. Why do production libraries use insertion sort here instead of merge sort?
options: Insertion sort has a better worst-case complexity on small inputs
Merge sort is only correct above a minimum array size
At n = 20 you are left of the crossover, where merge sort's larger constants and extra allocation outweigh its better growth rate
Insertion sort becomes O(n log n) when the input is small
mcqs.explanation: Asymptotic advantage only applies past the crossover point; below it the constant factors decide, and insertion sort does no allocation and touches memory sequentially. Its worst case is still O(n²) — the complexity class doesn't change with input size, only which algorithm wins in practice does.
